Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: A family member has a new job and has shared some initial excitement about it with their relatives.
Expectation2: Stay updated on changes in laws and legal precedents.
Situation2: In the middle of jury instructions, your clerk hands you an alert that the Supreme Court has just issued a ruling that directly overturns the key precedent your current instructions are based on. You must stop immediately.
Story: I was sitting in my chambers, reviewing my notes for the jury instructions, when my phone buzzed with a message from my daughter: “Dad, can you call tonight? Jamie wants to tell you about her new job!” I smiled, picturing my granddaughter’s eager face, and promised myself I’d call as soon as court ended. Moments later, in the courtroom, I was halfway through the instructions when my clerk rushed over, whispering that the Supreme Court had just overturned the very precedent I was explaining. My heart pounded. I knew I had to stop, review the new ruling, and possibly redo everything. The weight of the courtroom’s expectations pressed on me—every word I spoke had legal consequences. Yet, in the back of my mind, I could hear Jamie’s voice, waiting for her grandpa’s call, wanting to share her excitement. The demands of justice and family pulled at me, each urgent in its own way, and I stood there, torn, the gavel heavy in my hand.
